title: Contoso — Real-time AI customer support assistant
scenario: Contoso is building a customer support assistant that accepts text and image messages, transcribes voice messages, answers questions using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over a knowledge base, and routes escalations. The solution runs as a set of containerized microservices and must meet strict latency, cost, and compliance requirements.
context: The assistant must return grounded answers to chat messages in under 300 ms at the 95th percentile.
Compute must scale automatically with demand and scale to zero when idle to control cost.
Voice messages must be transcribed asynchronously and processed reliably in the background.
All service-to-service access must follow least privilege, and secrets must be rotated without redeploying.
Personally identifiable information (PII) in transcripts must not be exposed over the public internet.

sections.title: Overview
content: Contoso serves customers in multiple regions with a chat interface on web and mobile.
The assistant ingests text, image attachments, and voice messages.
Answers are generated by a large language model and must cite the source document they are grounded in.
Escalated conversations are handed to a human agent queue.

sections.title: Requirements
content: Latency: chat responses must be produced within 300 ms at p95; voice transcription is allowed up to 30 seconds.
Cost: non-production environments and the transcription worker must scale to zero when idle.
Security: use managed identities everywhere; never store API keys in code or in environment variables committed to source.
Compliance: transcriptions containing PII must only be accessible from the private virtual network.
Operations: trace every request end to end and alert when the answer quality signal degrades.

sections.title: Existing Environment
content: The knowledge base currently lives in a PostgreSQL database with the pgvector extension.
Model inference microservices are built as container images and pushed to Azure Container Registry.
A single Azure Kubernetes Service cluster hosts the services today, but the team wants to reduce operational overhead.
An Azure OpenAI resource and an Azure AI Speech resource are provisioned.

questions.prompt: Which compute service should Contoso use to run the containerized inference microservices so they scale on queue depth, scale to zero when idle, and avoid managing Kubernetes?
options: Azure Container Apps with KEDA scale rules and scale-to-zero enabled.
Azure Kubernetes Service with the cluster autoscaler.
Azure Container Instances with a restart policy of Always.
Azure App Service with CPU autoscale rules.
questions.explanation: Container Apps natively supports KEDA-based scaling (including queue-depth scalers) and scale-to-zero without operating Kubernetes. AKS requires cluster management, ACI does not autoscale on queue depth, and App Service scales on platform metrics rather than queue depth.

docs.label: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

questions.domain: Develop AI solutions by using Azure data management services
questions.prompt: Contoso wants chat answers to be grounded in source documents and returned with citations while supporting both keyword and semantic search over the knowledge base. Which service should provide the search and retrieval layer?
options: Azure AI Search with a hybrid (BM25 + vector) index and semantic ranking.
Azure Blob Storage with full-text search enabled.
Azure Cache for Redis with a TTL-based cache.
Azure Service Bus with message sessions.
questions.explanation: Azure AI Search provides integrated hybrid retrieval (keyword + vector) and semantic ranking in a single index designed for RAG grounding and citations. Blob Storage, Redis, and Service Bus do not provide this search capability.

questions.domain: Connect to and consume Azure services
questions.prompt: Voice messages must be transcribed in the background, retried on transient failure, and moved to a dead-letter queue after repeated failures for manual inspection. Which service should queue the transcription jobs?
options: Azure Event Grid with a system topic.
Azure Service Bus queue with Peek-Lock and MaxDeliveryCount configured.
Azure Event Hubs with Capture enabled.
Azure Queue Storage with receive-and-delete.
questions.explanation: Service Bus queues provide reliable delivery with retries (Peek-Lock) and automatic dead-lettering after MaxDeliveryCount is exceeded, preserving the reason for later inspection. Event Grid and Event Hubs lack per-message dead-lettering, and Queue Storage receive-and-delete loses messages on failure.

questions.domain: Secure, monitor, and troubleshoot Azure solutions
questions.prompt: Contoso must authenticate all microservices to Azure OpenAI, Azure AI Speech, and the PostgreSQL database without API keys, and keep transcriptions with PII off the public internet. Which combination should you use?
options: System-assigned managed identities on each service and a public endpoint on the speech resource.
A shared service principal with a client secret and public network access.
User-assigned managed identities with least-privilege roles, and private endpoints for the services that process PII.
API keys stored in application settings and a VNet service endpoint only.
questions.explanation: User-assigned managed identities enable per-service, least-privilege access with no stored keys, and private endpoints keep PII-bearing services off the public internet. System-assigned identities (option 0) still leave the speech resource public; a shared client secret (option 1) is insecure; stored API keys (option 3) violate the no-keys requirement.

title: Fabrikam — Streaming fraud detection pipeline
scenario: Fabrikam operates a payment platform that scores transactions for fraud in real time. A scoring microservice must evaluate every transaction in under 100 ms, features are stored as high-dimensional vectors, and a nightly batch job retrains the model. The system must handle bursts of millions of events and detect model drift.
context: Every transaction must be scored in under 100 ms.
The system must absorb bursts of millions of payment events without losing data.
Feature vectors must be stored and queried with filters for near-real-time retrieval.
The model must be retrained nightly and its behavior monitored for drift.
Container images must be rebuilt automatically when the base image or source code changes.

sections.title: Overview
content: Fabrikam's payment gateway emits a stream of transaction events.
A scoring microservice enriches each event with feature vectors and calls a fraud model.
A nightly job retrains the model on a dedicated GPU-enabled container and publishes a new image.
The compliance team requires full traceability of every model version used to score a transaction.

sections.title: Requirements
content: Latency: end-to-end scoring must complete within 100 ms at p99.
Throughput: the ingestion path must sustain millions of events per second during peak hours.
Retrieval: feature vectors must be looked up by transaction attributes and similarity.
Cost: the nightly training job must run only when scheduled and then terminate.
Governance: every scored transaction must record which model version produced the score.

sections.title: Existing Environment
content: Feature vectors are currently stored in a flat file store that cannot meet the latency target.
Images are built manually on a developer workstation and pushed to Azure Container Registry.
The scoring microservice runs in a fixed-size Azure Kubernetes Service node pool.
No drift detection is currently in place.

questions.domain: Develop AI solutions by using Azure data management services
questions.prompt: Fabrikam must store high-dimensional feature vectors and retrieve them by both scalar filters and similarity with sub-100 ms latency. Which data platform should you choose?
options: Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL with a vector index and a well-chosen partition key.
Azure Blob Storage with an access tier of Hot.
Azure Queue Storage polled by a timer function.
Azure Event Hubs with a consumer group.
questions.explanation: Cosmos DB for NoSQL stores high-dimensional vectors and supports vector similarity search combined with scalar filters, with low-latency point reads via a good partition key. Blob Storage, Queue Storage, and Event Hubs are not vector search engines.

docs.label: Vector search in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL

questions.prompt: The nightly training job must build a GPU-enabled image automatically when the CUDA base image or the training source code changes, reusing cached layers, then run and exit. Which two capabilities should you combine?
options: ACR Tasks with base-image-update and source commit triggers, and Azure Container Apps Jobs with a schedule trigger.
Manual docker build with --no-cache and an Azure Virtual Machine scheduled task.
Azure Kubernetes Service with a CronJob and a self-hosted build agent.
Azure App Service with WebJobs and local image builds.
questions.explanation: ACR Tasks rebuilds images automatically on base-image or commit changes while reusing cached layers, and Container Apps Jobs runs the image to completion on a schedule, paying only while it runs. The other options add manual build infrastructure or keep the job running continuously.

questions.domain: Connect to and consume Azure services
questions.prompt: Fabrikam must ingest millions of payment events per second, preserve per-merchant ordering, and allow multiple consumers to read the stream independently. Which service should you use?
options: Azure Service Bus queue with sessions.
Azure Queue Storage.
Azure Event Hubs with a partition key set to the merchant ID and multiple consumer groups.
Azure Event Grid with a system topic.
questions.explanation: Event Hubs provides high-throughput ingestion, partition-key ordering (per merchant), and consumer groups for independent readers. Service Bus and Queue Storage are not built for this ingestion scale, and Event Grid routes discrete events rather than a high-volume stream.

questions.domain: Secure, monitor, and troubleshoot Azure solutions
questions.prompt: Fabrikam must detect when the fraud model's accuracy drifts and record the model version for every scored transaction. Which approach should you use?
options: Log the model version as a custom dimension and configure an Azure Monitor alert on a custom metric that measures model accuracy.
Manually review a daily export of raw transactions in Excel.
Enable only Azure Activity Log monitoring.
Store scores in a local file on each replica and alert via email.
questions.explanation: Recording the model version as a custom dimension and alerting on a custom accuracy metric in Azure Monitor provides automated, traceable drift detection. Manual review (option 1) is not automated, Activity Log (option 2) is control-plane only, and local files (option 3) are not a monitoring solution.
